content: The implementation of a comprehensive strategy for leprosy eradication requires consensus on long-term planning, annual action plans, and budget allocation. This can be significantly facilitated by organizing joint actions at both global and regional levels. 1. At the global level, it is essential to sustain and enhance existing partnerships that promote leprosy-related actions. Mechanisms should be established to improve coordination among partners, such as global platforms or alliances. Regional training centers, remote help desks, medical research institutions, and rehabilitation hubs should also be leveraged to strengthen efforts. 2. Evidence must be generated regarding the involvement of private healthcare providers in leprosy care. Implementation research should be promoted to encourage their participation through structured partnerships and collaborations. 3. In high-burden settings, coalitions against leprosy should be established, involving all stakeholders to raise awareness and improve coordination. Civil society organizations, community representatives, patients, and families should be actively engaged in planning, service delivery, monitoring, and educational activities. Support for patients and their families, as well as advocacy and research, should also be prioritized. 4. A robust response to end leprosy and address the stagnation in case reduction requires the establishment of enduring partnerships across health and social sectors, as well as between healthcare systems and communities. 5. Research efforts must be maximized to inform policies, strategies, and activities. Despite the discovery of the causative agent of leprosy in 1873 by Dr. Armauer Hansen, significant gaps remain in understanding its transmission and pathogenesis. The inability to cultivate the organism in the laboratory and the limited understanding of immunological mechanisms leading to disabilities highlight the need for further research. 6. Although antibiotics for leprosy are widely accessible and free of charge, treatment for immunological reactions remains partial, and the drugs used do not completely halt these reactions. Effective preventive measures require more evidence, and research into the social aspects of leprosy is still limited. 7. To achieve the goal of leprosy elimination and eventual eradication, substantial investments are needed in research areas such as transmission, diagnosis (both of infection and disease), treatment of reactions, social integration, prevention, and alternative chemotherapies. Unfortunately, health research is often underfunded, creating a bottleneck in expanding research activities and strengthening capacity. 8. A comprehensive research strategy, including collaborative mechanisms, unified priorities, and capacity-building plans, would attract funding from domestic and international sources. Governments and partners should focus on mobilizing more resources for research activities while allocating an appropriate proportion of funding to operational research. 9. Globally, leprosy has benefited from large-scale research studies supported by the Tropical Diseases Research program of the WHO. However, funding for such initiatives has significantly declined in recent years. The Leprosy Research Initiative, launched in 2013, has provided approximately $4 million to date, supporting over 20 projects with a total funding of around €5 million. 10. Coordination among research institutions and national programs remains limited, necessitating the establishment of a global platform to set priorities and serve as a venue for scientists interested in leprosy research. National research priorities should be developed collaboratively with all partners in the national research network, ensuring a balance between research types and topics. These priorities should be periodically updated and integrated into national, regional, and global research plans. 11. Preventive tools, such as post-exposure prophylaxis with rifampicin and/or the BCG vaccine, are areas of interest in research. While the efficacy of rifampicin for contacts of leprosy patients has been proven, feasibility studies and implementation research are ongoing in multi-country settings. The results of these studies could guide programs on the use of available tools and monitoring their impact. 12. The Leprosy Research Initiative focuses on five research priorities: early detection of leprosy, prevention and treatment of nerve function impairment and reactions, social inclusion of affected individuals, prevention of disability, and methods to interrupt transmission and incidence. These priorities aim to increase the coverage of effective contact management and chemoprophylaxis. 13. At the global and regional levels, actions should include increasing resources for research through diversified funding sources, coordinating research through a global platform, identifying research centers to translate priorities into studies, and analyzing the results of research to incorporate new technologies and strategies into services. 14. In all settings, national research priorities should be established, and strategic capacity-building activities should be planned to increase human resources for leprosy health research. In low-burden settings, formal links with regional and global centers should be created to ensure the conduct of regional studies. 15. Surveillance and health information systems are critical for effective leprosy control. High-quality data is essential for assessing disease epidemiology and planning targeted activities. An ideal health information system should be case-based, allow reporting by all service providers, and enable analysis of data by geographical area, sex, age, and other factors. It should also facilitate drug management, contact screening, and record leprosy-related disabilities. 16. At the global level, strengthening surveillance and response monitoring systems is necessary. This includes engaging regional offices to facilitate data collection, supporting the development or adaptation of interoperable health information systems, and promoting integrated systems within existing platforms for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) and communicable diseases. 17. Efforts to stop leprosy and its complications should focus on early detection in high-burden areas, surveillance of drug resistance, and a stronger emphasis on disability prevention and management. Specific efforts should target early detection and treatment of children, including a critical incident investigation approach for each child with Grade 2 disability. 18. Achieving a leprosy-free world requires zero transmission, monitored through trends in age-specific case detection and transmission among nationals versus foreign-born cases. Efforts to interrupt transmission and prevent disease development among high-risk groups, including research on post-exposure prophylaxis, are encouraged. 19. The use of new e-tools to sustain knowledge and facilitate diagnosis, which often requires expertise and differential diagnosis with other NTDs and skin diseases, is promoted. Awareness of leprosy and other NTDs should be sustained, with activities suggested to improve understanding and encourage community involvement. 20. Messages about leprosy should be objective, positive, specific, and sensitive to age, gender, location, language, and culture. They should emphasize curability, the availability of free drugs, early signs, and the removal of stigma and discrimination. Core messages should encourage support and positivity towards affected individuals.
